AI AI Agent Productivity Software Development Product Management I Built an Open-Source, Local-First Workbench to Coordinate AI Coding Agents Sourik 5 min read · Oct 17, 2026 -- Listen Share Accession Workbench demo AI coding assistants have changed how I develop software. Instead of writing every line manually, I can ask an AI model to propose an implementation, generate code, review changes, or help diagnose failing tests. But as I started using more models and tools, I noticed a different problem. Writing code was becoming easier. Coordinating the work was not. A feature might involve several dependent tasks. One model could help design the implementation, another could write code, and another could review the result. But I still had to answer questions such as: Which task should run first? Which model is eligible for this task? Which agent is responsible? Which files may it change? What happens when the tests fail? How do I know the implementation is actually complete? Where do I keep the execution history? I wanted to connect these activities without introducing another mandatory cloud service. So I started building Accension . It’s an open-source, local-first AI model-routing and engineering orchestration platform written in Python. GitHub: https://github.com/Jigsaw777/accension Press enter or click to view image in full size Demo with mock models From model routing to an engineering Workbench The initial version of Accension focused on selecting AI models based on capabilities, quality evidence, privacy policies, and spending limits. The idea was straightforward: different tasks may benefit from different models, and routing should be governed by explicit constraints rather than an arbitrary recommendation. Version 1.1.0 extends that foundation with Accension Workbench . Workbench introduces persistent projects, structured Product Requirements Documents (PRDs), Work Items, dependencies, agent assignments, execution attempts, and completion review. The important architectural decision was to reuse the existing execution engine instead of building a separate task executor. 1. Start with requirements, not prompts Consider a simple feature: “Create a greeting function that handles named and blank inputs, with tests and documentation.” Instead of executing one large prompt, the requirement can be represented as a structured PRD. The PRD defines the objective, scope, functional requirements, and acceptance criteria. After reviewing the PRD, the work can be decomposed into smaller Work Items. For example: Implement the greeting function. Add tests covering named and blank inputs. Document how to use it. These tasks can have dependencies. That matters because code execution should not be scheduled purely by the order in which tasks appear on a screen. 2. Make dependencies explicit Accension represents executable task plans using its existing AXIR and ExecutionPlan contracts. The Workbench adds a persistent management layer above those plans. This distinction is useful. A Work Item represents an engineering obligation that can survive a restart or multiple execution attempts. An execution plan represents bounded work that can be carried out by the engine. The Workbench stores Work Item state and relationships while the existing execution infrastructure performs eligible, approved work. This avoids making the Kanban board a second execution engine. 3. Separate AI recommendations from authorization An AI model can propose how to divide a feature and what capabilities a worker should have. But a recommendation is not authorization. Accension applies eligibility, privacy, budget, repository permissions and execution-policy checks. In the Workbench, these concepts remain separate: Agent: A configured worker. Model: An inference backend. Router: The component that determines eligible models. Execution approval: A human decision authorizing the reviewed scope. The goal is to make assignments explainable and prevent an AI-generated plan from silently expanding its own permissions. 4. Treat validation as a separate engineering step One of the most important lessons from working with coding assistants is that a model’s final message isn’t reliable proof of completion. An AI can report success even when code fails to compile, tests fail, or the requirements were only partially implemented. Accension therefore records actual execution attempts and independent host-side validation. The system can preserve artifacts and execution receipts that describe what happened. Where human completion review is required, passing checks are necessary evidence but do not independently authorize completion. The Workbench also distinguishes PRD approval, task import, execution approval, and completion review. Those are different decisions. 5. Keep the architecture local-first Accension uses a Python backend, FastAPI, and SQLite with WAL storage. Its CLI, Workbench UI, and MCP interfaces interact with shared local application state. This design keeps installation relatively lightweight and avoids requiring a separate hosted database or message broker. The application can use local models, including through compatible local runtimes such as Ollama. It can also use configured cloud providers. That introduces an important privacy distinction: local project storage does not automatically mean all inference is local . Authorized cloud requests can send permitted context outside the computer.
